quote: includes _links to other documents_ as inline elements rather than appendices
problem: The HTML entry says what HTML is for but never what it is: "markup" and "inline elements" are never explained, so the reader cannot picture how a link sits inside a document that p8 then calls "just text".
fix: one tiny example: a few words wrapped in a tag that carries a URL
reason: Low severity but real. p4 is the only place the book says what HTML is, and 'inline elements rather than appendices' is jargon with no picture behind it; nowhere in Part III is a link ever shown inside a document, and p8 then calls HTML 'just text'. One tiny example fixes both.
judge_fix: Replace the HTML bullet's second sentence in ch11-bernerslee-p4 with: "A simple text format in which a link is written inside the sentence it belongs to, wrapped in tags that carry the target URL: `the project`."

quote: the long empty stretch is the quiet, the cluster at the bottom is the take-off
problem: In the drawing the long empty stretch runs from Dec 1991 to Apr 1993, but the label "2½ quiet years, one machine" sits on the Mar 1989 to Aug 1991 band. The reader cannot tell which stretch is the quiet one, or what happened between the announcement and the giveaway.
fix: point the strip at the labelled band, or name the 1992 gap
reason: Verified in the screenshot (fig-11-1-375-t6.667.png). The label '2½ quiet years, one machine' sits on the blue bar from Mar 1989 to Aug 1991. The long empty stretch is Dec 1991 to Apr 1993, below the California dot. The strip says the empty stretch is the quiet, so it contradicts the drawing and the caption.
judge_fix: Rewrite the first bullet of the Fig 11.1 strip: "*The scale.* Each dot sits at its date. The blue bar is the quiet: two and a half years from the proposal to the announcement, with one machine. The green bar at the bottom is the take-off after the giveaway." Do not claim nothing happened in 1992; the strip only needs to point at the labelled band.

quote: There was no Web Consortium yet, no licence, no fee.
problem: If joining was free from the start, the reader cannot see why the caption has the web taking off only after CERN gave the software away in April 1993. Nothing says what the software's status was before that.
fix: a clause: until April 1993 CERN owned the code and could still have charged for it
reason: p8 says 'no licence, no fee', yet the caption and p11 make the April 1993 release the turning point. The reader is never told that until then the code was still CERN's, with nothing in writing to stop CERN from charging. 'No licence' is also loose, because CERN held the copyright. CERN's 30 April 1993 statement relinquished its rights; before that the code was CERN property.
judge_fix: In ch11-bernerslee-p8 change "no Web Consortium yet, no licence, no fee" to "no Web Consortium yet and no fee to join". In the 1993 insight strip (p11) add after the first sentence: "Until that day the code was still CERN's property, free in practice but with nothing in writing to stop CERN from charging for it."

quote: the link broke and the publisher was supposed to update it
problem: As written, Xanadu's links break too, so the reader cannot see what Xanadu demanded that the web does not, or why that demand means "a central authority".
fix: say the link system was one shared register that every link and target had to join, run by someone, and that this is what kept links working
reason: As written, Xanadu's links break and the publisher repairs them, which is what the web does too, so the contrast with 'a central authority' does not follow. It is also a weak account of Xanadu: its design promised links that never break, by making every document register with one shared system that kept them working. That register is the central authority, and p9 should say so.
judge_fix: Replace the Xanadu sentence in ch11-bernerslee-p9 with: "In Project Xanadu, every document had to be registered with one shared link system, and that system, not the publisher, was meant to keep every link working; someone had to run the register and decide what went into it." Keep the rest of the paragraph as it is.

quote: it performs about twenty separate operations across four layers
problem: Fig 11.3 shows four exchanges (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP), nothing that adds up to twenty, and they are not the four TCP/IP layers of Fig 8.12, which puts DNS and HTTP in the same Application layer, so the reader can't line the claim up with the picture.
fix: say 'four exchanges in a row', matching the caption, or name the twenty
reason: 'About twenty operations across four layers' is not backed by anything on the page. Fig 11.3 and its caption show four exchanges (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP). Those are not the four TCP/IP layers of Fig 8.12, which put DNS and HTTP in the same Application layer. The number cannot be lined up with the picture.
judge_fix: In ch11-http-p6: "The browser does not \"open the page\": it runs four exchanges one after another, and the page appears only at the end."

quote: One curl, fully traced
problem: The figure title, its picture and its strip all rely on 'curl', which the book has not introduced, and the prose just before is about a browser, so the reader can't tell what a curl is or why the client changed.
fix: a gloss: curl, a command-line program that fetches one URL and prints the reply
reason: 'curl' appears in the figure title, picture and strip, but the book never introduces it. The surrounding prose is about a browser, so the reader does not know what a curl is or why the client changed.
judge_fix: Append to ch11-http-p6: "Fig 11.3 traces the same trip with `curl`, a command-line program that fetches one URL and prints the reply."

quote: Caches assume safety; retry logic assumes idempotency.
problem: The reader knows CPU caches but has never been told what a cache on the network path does (keeps a reply and answers a repeat request itself, so the server never sees it), so they can't explain why a cache needs safe requests; the retry half is shown in Fig 11.4, the cache half never is.
fix: one clause: a cache answers a repeat GET from its stored copy, so only a request that changes nothing can be answered that way
reason: p8 uses 'caches' as part of the contract on the network path, but the book has only taught CPU and page caches. It never says what a cache on the path does. The Fig 11.4 strip explains it only after the claim, and only if opened. One clause makes 'caches assume safety' derivable.
judge_fix: In ch11-http-p8 replace "Caches assume safety; retry logic assumes idempotency." with: "Caches assume safety (a cache answers a repeat `GET` from its stored copy without asking the server, which is only allowed for a request that changes nothing); retry logic assumes idempotency."

quote: because HTTP itself does not guarantee what its method properties promise
problem: The double charge happened with a POST, which the section says promises no idempotency at all, so the reader re-reads looking for a promise that was broken and finds none; the 'because' doesn't follow from the example.
fix: say POST promises nothing about a resend, and the key adds that promise; or that method properties are promises the server's code has to keep, which nothing in HTTP enforces
reason: The closing 'because' does not follow from the example. The double charge happens with a POST, and p8 already says POST promises no idempotency, so the reader looks for a broken promise and finds none. The real reason is that HTTP gives a POST no protection against repeats and the network can cause repeats.
judge_fix: In ch11-http-p10 replace "because HTTP itself does not guarantee what its method properties promise, and the network is not entirely reliable" with "because HTTP itself gives a POST no protection against being sent twice, and the network is not entirely reliable".

quote: discovered a practical, fast variant that worked against essentially every DNS resolver
problem: The paragraph names Kaminsky's variant but never says what it was. Guessing one 16-bit ID (65,536 tries) already sounds easy, so this reader cannot tell why the 1990s attack was only theoretical. The text never says that a lost race leaves the real answer cached for the TTL, which gives the attacker one try per name per TTL.
fix: one sentence: a failed guess caches the real answer, so Kaminsky asked for fresh made-up names (1.bank.com, 2.bank.com, ...), turning every one into a new race whose forged reply names the attacker as bank.com's server
reason: The paragraph's story is 'known in theory, made practical in 2008', but never says what made it practical. A 16-bit ID sounds easy to guess, so the reader cannot see why the 1990s attack was only theoretical. The missing point is that a failed guess left the real answer cached for the TTL, so one try per name per TTL. Kaminsky asked for names that cannot be cached, so every query was a new race. His forged replies also named the attacker's server as the authority for the whole domain.
judge_fix: In ch11-dns-p7, after "worked against essentially every DNS resolver in deployment", add: "Until then a failed guess was costly, because the real answer then sat in the cache and the name could not be raced again for the TTL; Kaminsky asked for fresh made-up names (`1.bank.com`, `2.bank.com`, and so on), each a new race, and let every forged reply also claim that the attacker's server ran all of `bank.com`."

quote: added source port randomisation, multiplying the attacker's guessing space from 2¹⁶ to 2³²
problem: The book has never explained what a transport port is; it has only shown ports as header numbers (53, 80, 51234). This paragraph also said only the ID has to match. So the reader cannot see why a forged reply must reach the port the query left from, that resolvers used to keep that port fixed, or why randomising it adds 16 bits. The fig 11.7 label gives the 16 bits only after the paragraph.
fix: a clause: a port is a 16-bit number that picks the receiving program; a reply is accepted only at the port the query came from, which resolvers used to keep fixed
reason: A transport port is never explained in prose anywhere in the book. In ch8 to ch10 it appears only as a header field in the UDP figure, in the SYN-cookie tuple and in a NAT label. The whole defence in p7 and Fig 11.7 ('16-bit ID x 16-bit port') depends on it. The reader cannot see why a forged reply must hit the port the query left from, or why randomising it adds 16 bits. This is a gap from Chapter 10, but the cheapest repair is at its first load-bearing use here.
judge_fix: In ch11-dns-p7, before the Kaminsky sentence or at the port sentence, add: "A query leaves the resolver from a port, a 16-bit number the operating system uses to hand each reply to the right program, and a reply is accepted only if it arrives at that port; resolvers then used the same port every time, so only the ID had to be guessed." Optionally add one line on ports to ch10-udp-p1 or p2 as the better home.

quote: (duplicate response, wrong source)
problem: Low severity. This label sits under '→ ignores real answer' and says the real reply comes from the wrong source. The real reply comes from the real server's address, the same address the attacker spoofed. The resolver drops it only because the query has already been answered.
fix: owner's call (kept-original); the accurate reading is 'duplicate response: query already answered'
reason: Fig 11.7 is kept-original and a factual slip is real. The real answer arrives from the real server's address, the one the attacker spoofed, so 'wrong source' is incorrect. The resolver drops it because the query is already answered. The caption and the figure otherwise agree. Only the owner can change the label.
judge_fix: Owner's call. If changed, make the label read "(duplicate response: query already answered)".

quote: The signature, made with the certificate's private key, proves the server is who
problem: Section 04 (ch11-crypto-p7, Fig 11.10) taught only that the public key locks and the private key unlocks. The book never explains what a digital signature is, or how something made with a private key gets checked with the public key and so proves identity. Neither this section nor any earlier one does, yet the chain check at ch11-tls-p4 and the Fig 11.12 caption ('checks each signature with the public key of the certificate above it') rests on it.
fix: one sentence on first use: a signature is computed with the private key over the data's hash; anyone can check it with the public key, and only the key's holder could have made it
reason: The section never says what a signature is, yet tls-p2, the Fig 11.11 strip and the whole chain check at p4 and Fig 11.12 rest on it. The only thing taught before is 'public locks, private unlocks'. Fig 14.12 explains signatures, but that is a later part. One sentence in the crypto briefing, where the book says TLS needs the primitives, fixes it for every later use.
judge_fix: Add to ch11-crypto-p7 after the sentence on the key pair: "The pair has a second use, the *digital signature*: the key's owner computes a value from a message's hash with the private key, anyone can check it with the public key, and only the owner could have produced it."

quote: its very first reply: certificate, signature and all
problem: p2 leans on the certificate (what it 'says', and 'the certificate's private key') before the reader knows a certificate is a signed file that binds the server's name to its public key. That is explained later at ch11-tls-p4. Earlier pages only name certificates in passing (ch10-attacks-p8, ch11-crypto-p4).
fix: a half-clause at first use: the certificate, a signed file binding the server's name to its public key (more below)
reason: p2 leans on 'the certificate' and 'the certificate's private key' before the reader knows it is a signed file tying a server's name to its public key. The explanation comes two paragraphs later at p4, and earlier chapters only mention certificates in passing. A half-clause at first use is enough.
judge_fix: In ch11-tls-p2 change "certificate, signature and all" to "the certificate (a signed file tying the server's name to its public key, unpacked below) and a signature, all".

quote: Each Finished is a MAC over the whole transcript, so tampering shows.
problem: This reader knows MAC only as the Ethernet MAC address (ch8-ethernet), a hardware identifier. The book never introduces a message authentication code (a hash keyed with the shared secret), and p2 called the same thing plain 'a hash of the entire transcript', so the strip reads as a contradiction.
fix: 'a hash keyed with the shared secret (a MAC, message authentication code)', or just 'a keyed hash'
reason: The reader knows MAC only as the hardware address of Ch 8. A message authentication code appears nowhere in the book before this strip (HMAC shows up only in Part IV). p2 calls the same thing 'a hash of the entire transcript', so the strip reads as a different mechanism.
judge_fix: In the Fig 11.11 strip replace "Each Finished is a MAC over the whole transcript, so tampering shows." with "Each Finished is a hash of the whole transcript keyed with the shared secret (a MAC, message authentication code), so tampering shows." Optionally say "a keyed hash of the entire transcript" in tls-p2 to match.

quote: Neither is a new HTTP: the headers, methods, and status codes
problem: The section title says these upgrades 'broke compatibility on purpose', but the body only says the HTTP layer is unchanged. It never says what broke: an HTTP/1.1-only server cannot read binary frames, and QUIC needs UDP to get through. Nor does it say how a browser and server agree on a version, which matters because ch11-http-p1 promised that HTTP/1.0 still works against modern servers.
fix: one sentence: old software cannot read the new packing, so browser and server first agree on a version (inside the TLS handshake; HTTP/3 is advertised by the server and then tried), and the speed was worth that break
reason: Low severity. The section title promises broken compatibility, but p1 stresses what is unchanged and only p2 and p5 imply the break. The reader is not told how an old server and a new browser cope, even though ch11-http-p1 promised HTTP/1.0 still works. The negotiation mechanism is standard: ALPN inside the TLS handshake for HTTP/2; the server advertises HTTP/3 and the browser tries it and falls back.
judge_fix: Add to ch11-modern-p1 after "carried.": "The new packing is unreadable to old software, so browser and server first agree on a version (HTTP/2 inside the TLS handshake; HTTP/3 is advertised by the server and then tried) and fall back to HTTP/1.1 when the other side cannot; the speed was worth that break."

quote: pushing the attack from "a few minutes" to "years."
problem: Port randomisation made forging about 65,000 times harder, but it did not push the attack out to years. Kaminsky's attack on an unpatched resolver took about 10 seconds. In August 2008 Evgeniy Polyakov poisoned a patched BIND 9.5.0-P2, with about 64,000 random ports, in a little under 10 hours, using two machines on a gigabit link; the estimate before his demonstration was about a week. The reader is left thinking the patched attack is out of reach, which the sentence before ('did not fix the underlying weakness') rightly denies.
fix: "...multiplying the attacker's guessing space from 2¹⁶ to 2³² and turning seconds of flooding into hours or days of it." Sources: Polyakov's write-up (exploit-db.com/raw/6236, "a bit less than 10 hours"); Slashdot/NYT (Markoff), 9 Aug 2008, "BIND Still Susceptible To DNS Cache Poisoning".
reason: Checked Polyakov's write-up (exploit-db 6236): a patched BIND was poisoned in 'a bit less than 10 hours' using two servers on a GigE link. 'Years' is false and contradicts the sentence before it. Unpatched Kaminsky attack took seconds, so 'a few minutes' is also loose.
judge_fix: Replace '...multiplying the attacker's guessing space from 2¹⁶ to 2³² and pushing the attack from "a few minutes" to "years."' with: '...multiplying the attacker's guessing space from 2¹⁶ to about 2³² and stretching the attack from seconds of flooding to hours: that August a researcher poisoned a patched BIND in under ten hours.' Source: exploit-db.com/raw/6236 (Polyakov, 'a bit less than 10 hours'); Slashdot/NYT, 9 Aug 2008.

quote: pushed the practical attack from minutes to years
problem: This is the same overclaim as ch11-dns-p7, in the kept-original caption. A patched BIND was poisoned in under 10 hours in August 2008 (Polyakov), and the unpatched attack took seconds, not minutes. The figure is owner-kept, so this is reported only. If the prose is fixed, the caption will contradict it.
fix: If the owner allows a caption edit: "...showed how to make this practical against unpatched resolvers in seconds... multiplied the attacker's search space ~65,000-fold and pushed the practical attack from seconds to hours or days." Source: exploit-db.com/raw/6236.
reason: Fig 11.7 is in the kept_original list. The caption has the same overclaim ('from minutes to years'; the unpatched attack took seconds). Only the owner can allow a caption edit, and once p7 is fixed the two will disagree.
judge_fix: Flag to owner. If he allows an edit: '...showed how to make this practical against unpatched resolvers in seconds. The fix, randomising the source port as well as the transaction ID, multiplied the attacker's search space ~65,000-fold and pushed the practical attack from seconds to hours.' Source: exploit-db.com/raw/6236.

quote: if the target moved or disappeared, the link broke and the publisher was supposed to update it
problem: This gets Xanadu backwards. Nelson's design made links visible and followable from every endpoint (rule 7), gave every document a unique permanent identity (rule 10), let documents be found without knowing where they were stored (rule 12) and kept them redundantly (rule 14), all so that links could not break. Links breaking when a target moves is the web's behaviour (Xanadu attacks the web for its 'one-way ever-breaking links'). As written, the sentence takes away the very contrast the paragraph is drawing.
fix: "In Project Xanadu, links ran both ways and every document kept a permanent address that the system itself maintained, so no link could ever break; keeping that promise needed one system that tracked every link." Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Xanadu (Nelson's 17 rules; xanadu.com critique of the web).
reason: Xanadu's design (permanent addresses, two-way links kept by the system) was meant to make links unbreakable. Breaking links is the web's behaviour. The sentence inverts the contrast the paragraph relies on.
judge_fix: Replace 'In Project Xanadu, every link required the target document to formally register itself with the link system; if the target moved or disappeared, the link broke and the publisher was supposed to update it.' with: 'In Project Xanadu, every document had to live inside the link system, which kept its address permanent and tracked every link in both directions, so no link could ever break.' The rest of the paragraph (the 404, link rot, central authority) still follows. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Xanadu (Nelson's design rules).

quote: released the entire web (code, protocols, specifications) into the public domain, with a one-page document declaring no royalties
problem: The 30 April 1993 statement put three pieces of software into the public domain: the line-mode browser, the basic server and the library of common code. It says CERN 'relinquishes all intellectual property rights to this code' and lets anyone 'use, duplicate, modify and distribute it'. It does not cover protocols or specifications, and it says nothing about patents. The 'royalty-free' wording belongs to CERN's later 1994 licence.
fix: "On 30 April 1993 CERN put the web's software (the line-mode browser, the basic server and the library of common code) into the public domain, giving up all intellectual property rights so that anyone could use, copy, modify and redistribute it." Sources: home.cern/science/computing/the-birth-of-the-web/licensing-web/; Berners-Lee to www-talk, May 1993 (ksi.cpsc.ucalgary.ca/archives/WWW-TALK/www-talk-1993q2.messages/257.html).
reason: CERN's licensing page and the 1993 www-talk post say the declaration covered three pieces of software: the line-mode browser, the basic server and the common code library. It says nothing about protocols or specifications. The CERN page does not mention royalties or patents for 1993, and royalty-free wording belongs to the 1994 licence.
judge_fix: Replace the first sentence with: 'On 30 April 1993 CERN released the web's software (the line-mode browser, the basic server and the library of common code) into the public domain, giving up all intellectual property rights so that anyone could use, copy, modify and redistribute it.' Delete 'with a one-page document declaring no royalties were owed and no patents would be filed'. Sources: home.cern/science/computing/the-birth-of-the-web/licensing-web/; www-talk 1993q2 message 257.

quote: By the early 1980s the file had grown to thousands of entries
problem: The host table listed 213 hosts in August 1981, 235 in May 1982 and 562 in August 1983, the year DNS was designed. It passed 1,000 only in October 1984 and reached about 2,000 in 1985. The book's own Fig 9.2 draws '1981 · 213 hosts', so the two figures contradict each other.
fix: "By 1983 the file listed more than 500 hosts, roughly doubling each year, was edited by hand, and was copied out over the network." Source: RFC 1296 (Lottor, 1992), host-count table taken from the NIC host tables.
reason: Host counts in the NIC host tables were 213 (Aug 1981) and 562 (Aug 1983), and the book's own Fig 9.2 and UNDER.md line 557 use 213. 'Thousands' in the early 1980s contradicts them.
judge_fix: Replace 'By the early 1980s the file had grown to thousands of entries, was edited by hand,' with 'By 1983 the file listed more than 500 machines, was edited by hand,'. Source: RFC 1296 (Lottor, 1992) host-count table.

quote: Humans do not remember 93.184.216.34.
problem: With 'Something has to translate the second into the first', this says example.com resolves to 93.184.216.34. The §4g ledger (Fig 11.3 row) recorded that example.com has moved off that address and removed it from the figure. The prose brings the stale address back. On 15 Oct 2026, dig gives 104.20.23.154 and 172.66.147.243.
fix: "Humans do not remember a number like 203.0.113.7. Humans remember `example.com`. Something has to translate the name into its number..." (203.0.113.7 is a documentation address, RFC 5737, already used in Fig 11.7).
reason: The §4g ledger (Fig 11.3 row) dropped 93.184.216.34 because example.com moved. The prose still pairs it with example.com, and a reader who runs dig will see a different answer. It is the only occurrence in the book (public/part-3.html, line 3697).
judge_fix: Replace 'Humans do not remember 93.184.216.34. Humans remember `example.com`. Something has to translate the second into the first' with 'Humans do not remember numbers like 192.0.2.44. Humans remember `example.com`. Something has to translate the second into the first'. 192.0.2.44 is a documentation address (RFC 5737). Do not use 203.0.113.7 or 198.51.100.66, which Fig 11.7 uses for bank.com and the attacker.

quote: the certificates of Section 05 rely on it, and so does every TLS handshake
problem: TLS 1.3 handshakes negotiated with TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 use SHA-384 for the transcript hash and HKDF, not SHA-256. The §4g row for Fig 14.11 already corrected this point in Ch14 ('HKDF uses SHA-256 or SHA-384 by cipher suite').
fix: "...the certificates of Section 05 rely on it, and so do most TLS handshakes (the rest use its longer sibling, SHA-384)." Source: RFC 8446 §B.4 (cipher suites TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384).
reason: TLS 1.3 handshakes with TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 use SHA-384 (RFC 8446 App. B.4). 'Every' is an overclaim, and the Fig 14.11 ledger row already made the same correction elsewhere. A one-word repair.
judge_fix: Replace 'and so does every TLS handshake' with 'and so do most TLS handshakes'.

quote: a fingerprint of the data, uniquely identifying it without revealing it
problem: A 256-bit hash cannot identify inputs uniquely: inputs are unlimited, so collisions must exist. A hash works as a fingerprint because of collision resistance (nobody can find two inputs with the same hash), and the paragraph's list of 'three properties' leaves that out. Yet it is the property that certificates and Git IDs depend on, and why SHA-1 ('the older SHA-1', mentioned in the next sentence) was retired.
fix: "The hash is, in effect, a fingerprint of the data, identifying it because nobody can find two inputs with the same hash (collision resistance), and revealing nothing of it."
reason: A fixed 256-bit output cannot identify unlimited inputs uniquely. The property that makes a hash a fingerprint is collision resistance, and the next sentence invokes SHA-1's retirement. A careful reader will see this. Minimal repair, no new depth (law 4).
judge_fix: Replace 'uniquely identifying it without revealing it' with 'identifying it for every practical purpose without revealing it'.

quote: HTTP/1.1 from 1999 was good enough for nearly two decades.
problem: HTTP/1.1 was first standardised in RFC 2068 in January 1997. RFC 2616 (June 1999) was a revision. This also sits oddly next to 'HTTP/1.0 from 1996' in Section 02.
fix: "HTTP/1.1, from 1997, was good enough for nearly two decades." Source: RFC 2068 (January 1997), obsoleted by RFC 2616 (June 1999).
reason: HTTP/1.1 was first specified in RFC 2068 (January 1997); RFC 2616 (1999) revised it. Standard references date HTTP/1.1 to 1997.
judge_fix: Replace 'HTTP/1.1 from 1999 was good enough for nearly two decades.' with 'HTTP/1.1, from 1997, was good enough for nearly two decades.' Source: RFC 2068, obsoleted by RFC 2616.

quote: submitted a 17-page document to his manager
problem: CERN's archived copy of the March 1989 proposal (the one Sendall annotated) is a cover plus pages numbered 1 to 14, with one handwritten comment page: 16 scanned pages, 15 typed. The May 1990 reissue runs to 20 pages. I found no source for 17.
fix: Drop the count: "submitted a document to his manager titled _Information Management: A Proposal_." Source: repository.cern/records/6kxvc-v6203 (ARCH-WWW-4-010.pdf, 16 pages; dd-89-001.pdf, 20 pages).
reason: I could not find 17 pages in any source. CERN's and W3C's pages give no count, and the finding reports the archive scan as 16 pages (cover plus 1 to 14 plus the comment page). An unsourced precise number breaks the fact-ledger law, and the claim adds nothing.
judge_fix: Replace 'submitted a 17-page document to his manager titled' with 'submitted a document to his manager titled'.

quote: the dozen earlier hypertext systems that never caught on
problem: Not every earlier hypertext system failed to catch on. HyperCard (1987) came free with every Macintosh and was very widely used. What it lacked was links between computers.
fix: "One decision separates the web from the hypertext systems before it."
reason: 'Never caught on' is false for HyperCard (bundled with every Mac), Guide and Windows Help, and 'a dozen' is unsourced. The point of the sentence is the single decision, not the earlier systems' fate. Low severity.
judge_fix: Replace 'One decision separates the web from the dozen earlier hypertext systems that never caught on.' with 'One decision separates the web from the hypertext systems before it.'

problem: p1 "in Building 31 at CERN": the UNDER.md §4g row for Fig 11.1 (line 565) removed "CERN Building 31" from the figure as unsourced, but the prose still states it. Either source it or remove it from p1 as well (fact-ledger law).
reason: The ledger removed 'CERN Building 31' from Fig 11.1 as unsourced, yet p1 still states it. My search found only a CERN history page placing a Computing and Networking division office in building 31, which is not specific to the server. The prose and the ledger should agree.
judge_fix: Replace 'running on a black NeXT workstation in Building 31 at CERN.' with 'running on a black NeXT workstation at CERN.'

problem: p9 Xanadu: Nelson's design kept every document permanently at a fixed address, with two-way links held by the system, so its links were not supposed to break at all. "If the target moved or disappeared, the link broke and the publisher was supposed to update it" does not describe Xanadu.
reason: Duplicate of finding 3. The Xanadu description is inverted.
judge_fix: Same as finding 3.

problem: p9 "if the URL no longer resolves, the click gets back a 404": a 404 comes from a server that answers but has no document at that path. A URL that no longer resolves (its host name is gone) gets no 404, only a failure to connect. The next section teaches resolving, so readers will notice the mix-up.
reason: A 404 comes from a server that answers but has no document at that path. A URL whose host is gone fails with no HTTP answer at all, and Section 03 teaches resolving. The repair is a few words.
judge_fix: Replace 'if the URL no longer resolves, the click gets back a 404' with 'if the page behind the URL is gone, the click gets back a 404'.

problem: p11 "every later attempt to build a 'private web' (AOL, MSN, Compuserve...)": CompuServe (1979) and AOL (1989, from Quantum Link in 1985) ran their walled gardens before the 1993 release. Only MSN (1995) came later.
reason: CompuServe (1979) and AOL (1989) were walled gardens before the 1993 release. 'Every later attempt to build a private web' is wrong for them. They eventually opened onto the web.

problem: ch11-dns-p2 'By the early 1980s the file had grown to thousands of entries': the internet host count was about 213 in 1981 and 562 in August 1983. It passed 1,000 only in late 1984 and about 2,000 in 1985. 'Hundreds' fits the early 1980s; 'thousands' fits only the mid-1980s.

problem: ch11-dns-p1 'billions of times per second across the planet': no source is given. The largest public resolvers report on the order of a trillion queries a day, which is tens of millions per second. A global rate in the billions per second may be an order of magnitude or more too high.

problem: p4 'uniquely identifying it': inputs of any size go into a fixed 256-bit output, so the hash cannot be unique (endlessly many inputs share each hash). What makes it work as a fingerprint in practice is collision resistance: no one can find two inputs with the same hash. The three listed properties leave that out, and preimage resistance does not imply it.
reason: Duplicate of finding 8.
judge_fix: Same as finding 8.

problem: p4 'and so does every TLS handshake': TLS 1.3 handshakes can run on SHA-384 (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, the first suite in OpenSSL's default list), and some certificate chains are signed with SHA-384. 'Nearly every' would be safe.
reason: Duplicate of finding 7.
judge_fix: Same as finding 7.

Sec 04 teaches only lock with public / open with private, and the promise is 'enough to read the TLS handshake'. Part 3 has no earlier definition. 'The certificate's private key' is also loose, since a certificate holds only the public key.
judge_fix: ch11-crypto-p7, after 'can only be decrypted with the matching private key.', add: 'The pair also runs in reverse: a value computed from a message with the private key, which anyone can check with the public key but only the key's owner could have produced, is a *digital signature*.' tls-p2: 'The signature, made with the private key that matches the certificate's public key, proves the server is who the certificate says;'.
